category.name: BEC & payment fraud
category.description: Business email compromise and payment fraud: bank-detail changes, executive wire requests, payroll diversion, invoice tampering and fund recovery.

playbooks.name: Vendor bank-detail change request suspected to be fraudulent
playbooks.summary: Use when accounts payable received a request to change a supplier's remittance bank account and something is off: new domain, urgency, or a request outside the normal vendor portal.

preparation: Require call-back verification to a number already on file before any vendor bank change
Log every vendor master data change in the ERP with requester and approver
Give AP a direct line to the SOC for suspicious payment requests
identification: Compare the requesting address and domain with the vendor contact on file in the ERP
Check the message headers for lookalike domains, reply-to mismatches or failed DMARC
Call the vendor on the phone number in the vendor master, not the one in the email
List payments scheduled to that vendor in the next payment run
Check whether the vendor master record was already changed and by whom
containment: Place a hold on all pending payments to the vendor until the bank details are verified
Revert the vendor master bank fields if they were updated from the fraudulent request
Block the lookalike domain at the gateway
eradication: Tell the vendor their identity is being used and suggest they check their own mailbox for compromise
Search AP mailboxes for other bank change requests from the same domain
Remove the fraudulent sender from any AP mailbox safe-sender list
recovery: Release held payments after verification with the vendor by phone
Record the verified bank details with a note of who confirmed them and when
Brief AP staff on the indicators that caught this attempt
lessons: Confirm whether the call-back control was followed or skipped and why
Add a detection for inbound mail to AP that mentions bank details from a domain first seen this month
Track how many vendor bank change requests are verified per quarter

splunk.title: Mail to AP from the requesting domain
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as first from datamodel=Email where All_Email.recipient IN (<ap_mailboxes>) All_Email.src_user="*@<ioc_domain>" by All_Email.src_user All_Email.subject | convert ctime(first)

splunk.title: Vendor master changes in the ERP
splunk.spl: index=erp sourcetype=<erp_audit> object=vendor_master field IN (bank_account, iban, routing_number) earliest=-30d | table _time user vendor_id field old_value new_value

playbooks.name: Executive impersonation email requesting an urgent wire transfer
playbooks.summary: Use when finance received an urgent, confidential request appearing to come from the CEO or CFO to send a wire, often to a new beneficiary, before any money has moved.

preparation: Require dual approval and a verbal check with the requester for wires over a set threshold
Configure display-name impersonation protection for all executive names
Give finance a known-good phone list for executives
identification: Check whether the sender is the executive's real mailbox, a lookalike domain or a free webmail account
Contact the executive by a known phone number to confirm whether they sent it
Check the executive's real mailbox for compromise if the message came from it
Record the beneficiary bank, account number and amount requested
Search for the same sender contacting other finance staff
containment: Stop the wire in the treasury system if it is queued
Block the sender address and domain at the gateway
Warn the finance and treasury teams about the active attempt
eradication: Reset credentials for the executive if their real account sent the request
Report the beneficiary account to your bank's fraud team
Remove the lure and any follow-ups from finance mailboxes
recovery: Thank the staff member who escalated and share the outcome with finance
Confirm no other payments went to the beneficiary account in the last 90 days
Review open payment requests that cite the executive's authority
lessons: Record whether the wire threshold and verbal check rules were followed
Add a detection for external mail using an executive display name to finance staff
Run a short tabletop with finance on executive wire requests

splunk.title: Executive display name from external senders
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=ms:o365:reporting:messagetrace earliest=-14d NOT SenderAddress="*@<your_domain>" | search Subject IN ("*urgent*", "*wire*", "*confidential*", "*payment*") | stats count values(RecipientAddress) as recipients by SenderAddress Subject

splunk.title: Finance recipients of the sender
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src_user="<sender>" by All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.action

playbooks.name: Payroll diversion: employee direct deposit changed to attacker account
playbooks.summary: Use when an employee's pay was redirected to a new bank account, either through a fake email to HR or an attacker logging in to the payroll portal as the employee.

preparation: Require HR to confirm direct deposit changes by phone or in person, never by email
Notify the employee's old address and phone automatically when bank details change
Hold the first pay run after a bank change for verification
identification: Determine whether the change came by email to HR or through a self-service portal login
If by email, check whether it came from the employee's real mailbox or a lookalike
If by portal, review the login IP, device and MFA method used for the change
Confirm with the employee in person or by known phone number that they did not request it
Search for other direct deposit changes made from the same IP or sender
containment: Revert the employee's bank details and stop the pending payment if possible
Lock self-service bank changes for any account accessed from the attacker IP
Reset the employee's SSO and payroll portal credentials
eradication: Contact the payroll provider and bank to recall any deposit already sent
Remove attacker MFA devices from the employee's accounts
Block the lookalike domain or webmail sender used to contact HR
recovery: Arrange an off-cycle payment to the employee for any lost pay
Confirm the next pay run reaches the correct account
Keep the employee informed of the recall status
lessons: Record whether the bank-change notification reached the employee and when
Add a detection for portal bank changes from IPs not seen for that employee
Check whether the employee was phished earlier and link the cases

splunk.title: Payroll portal bank changes and their source IPs
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=<payroll_audit> action IN (bank_account_change, direct_deposit_update) earliest=-30d | stats count values(employee_id) as employees by src_ip user_agent | sort - count

splunk.title: HR mailbox requests about direct deposit
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.recipient IN (<hr_mailboxes>) All_Email.subject IN ("*direct deposit*", "*bank*", "*payroll*") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.subject

playbooks.name: Gift card purchase request impersonating a manager
playbooks.summary: Use when a staff member was asked by someone posing as their manager to buy gift cards and send the codes, whether or not any cards were bought.

preparation: State in policy and onboarding that managers never ask staff to buy gift cards
Turn on external sender tagging so webmail impersonation is obvious
Give staff a simple way to check with a manager by chat or phone
identification: Record the sender address, the manager impersonated and the phone number if SMS was used
Find out whether cards were bought, which brand and whether codes were sent
Search mail for the same sender writing to other staff
Check how the attacker learned the reporting line, such as a public org chart
containment: Contact the gift card brand's fraud line with the card numbers to freeze unused balances
Block the sender address at the gateway
Warn the impersonated manager's team about the attempt
eradication: Report the sender to the webmail provider's abuse team
Remove the lure from other mailboxes
Keep receipts and card numbers for any police or insurer report
recovery: Reimburse the staff member under the expense policy if management approves
Reassure the staff member that reporting quickly was the right step
Check back with the card issuer on whether balances were frozen
lessons: Track how many gift card lures were reported versus acted on
Review public sources that expose reporting lines and remove what is not needed
Add a detection for external mail containing gift card wording sent to staff

splunk.title: Gift card wording in external mail
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.subject IN ("*gift card*", "*quick favor*", "*are you available*") NOT All_Email.src_user="*@<your_domain>" by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject

splunk.title: Other targets of the sender
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=ms:o365:reporting:messagetrace SenderAddress="<sender>" | stats count values(Subject) as subjects by RecipientAddress

playbooks.name: Real vendor mailbox compromised and sending altered invoices
playbooks.summary: Use when invoices with changed bank details come from a supplier's genuine mailbox, because the supplier was compromised, so headers and domains all look legitimate.

preparation: Keep a security contact for top suppliers separate from their billing contacts
Flag invoices whose bank details differ from the vendor master automatically in the AP system
Retain inbound mail headers long enough to compare old and new messages from suppliers
identification: Compare bank details on the new invoice with previous paid invoices from the vendor
Check headers for the vendor's usual sending servers versus new IPs or client types
Call the vendor's security or finance lead on a known number to confirm compromise
Find all invoices and payment-related messages from the vendor in the last 60 days
Check whether any payment already went to the new account
containment: Hold all payments to the vendor until they confirm their mailbox is clean
Quarantine incoming mail from the vendor domain for review
Revert any vendor master bank changes made from these invoices
eradication: Share the suspicious headers with the vendor so they can investigate their mailbox
Ask the vendor to confirm the attacker's inbox rules and access have been removed
Request a signed letter on vendor letterhead confirming the correct bank details
recovery: Release held payments using the confirmed bank details
Lift the quarantine on the vendor domain after their remediation is confirmed
Start a recall with your bank for any payment already sent to the fraudulent account
lessons: Record whether the AP system flagged the bank detail mismatch
Add a detection for vendor mail arriving from new sending IPs or countries
Review which suppliers should be added to a vendor risk review

splunk.title: Sending IPs used by the vendor over time
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=ms:o365:reporting:messagetrace SenderAddress="*@<vendor_domain>" earliest=-90d | stats count min(_time) as first max(_time) as last by FromIP | convert ctime(first) ctime(last) | sort first

splunk.title: Invoice-related mail from the vendor
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src_user="*@<vendor_domain>" All_Email.subject IN ("*invoice*", "*payment*", "*remittance*", "*bank*") by All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.src_ip

playbooks.name: Attorney or law firm impersonation demanding a confidential payment
playbooks.summary: Use when someone posing as outside counsel or a regulator contacts finance about a secret deal, settlement or legal matter that needs an immediate payment and must not be discussed.

preparation: Keep a list of the company's retained law firms and their known contacts with general counsel
Tell finance that legal payments must be confirmed with the in-house legal team first
Enable impersonation checks for the domains of retained law firms
identification: Check the sender domain against the retained law firm list held by legal
Ask general counsel whether the matter, firm and attorney named are real
Record any phone numbers, call times and beneficiary details provided
Search for earlier contact from the same domain to finance or executives
containment: Cancel any payment prepared for the matter
Block the impersonating domain and phone numbers where possible
Tell finance leadership that the attempt is active
eradication: Inform the real law firm that its name is being used
Report the beneficiary account to your bank's fraud desk
Purge the lure messages from recipient mailboxes
recovery: Confirm with legal that no genuine matter was disrupted
Brief executives who might be named in follow-up attempts
Record the attempt in the fraud register for the auditors
lessons: Check whether secrecy wording in the request delayed escalation
Add a detection for lookalikes of retained law firm domains
Include legal-pretext scenarios in finance fraud training

splunk.title: Mail from law-firm lookalike domains
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src_user="*@<ioc_domain>" OR All_Email.subject IN ("*confidential*acquisition*", "*legal matter*", "*settlement*") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject

splunk.title: Prior contact from the domain
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=ms:o365:reporting:messagetrace SenderAddress="*@<ioc_domain>" earliest=-90d | stats count min(_time) as first values(Subject) as subjects by RecipientAddress | convert ctime(first)

playbooks.name: Real estate closing wire instructions altered before settlement
playbooks.summary: Use when a buyer, title company or escrow agent received changed wiring instructions for a property closing, and funds may be sent to an attacker instead of the escrow account.

preparation: Give every client the escrow wiring details in person at the start and say they will never change
Require a call to a known number before any closing wire is released
Monitor agent and escrow officer mailboxes for new forwarding rules
identification: Compare the altered instructions with the original escrow account details
Find out who sent the change and whether it came from a staff mailbox or a lookalike
Check the escrow officer's and agent's mailboxes for compromise and hidden rules
Confirm with the client whether funds were already wired and when
List other active closings handled by the same compromised mailbox
containment: Call the client's bank immediately to request a recall if funds were sent
Warn every client with an active closing handled by that mailbox by phone
Reset the compromised mailbox and revoke sessions
eradication: Remove forwarding rules and attacker access from the mailbox
File a complaint with the national cybercrime reporting center for wire fraud
Block the lookalike domain used in the altered instructions
recovery: Work with the title company and banks to reschedule the closing with verified instructions
Confirm the recall outcome with the receiving bank
Brief agents on the call-back step before the next closing
lessons: Record the time between wire and recall request and how it affected recovery
Add a detection for messages containing wire instructions sent from outside the escrow system
Decide whether closing instructions should only be delivered through a secure portal

splunk.title: Messages containing wiring instructions
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.subject IN ("*wire*instruction*", "*closing*", "*escrow*", "*updated*bank*") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject _time span=1d

splunk.title: Forwarding rules on escrow mailboxes
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=o365:management:activity Operation IN (New-InboxRule, Set-InboxRule, Set-Mailbox) UserId IN (<escrow_mailboxes>) earliest=-60d | table _time UserId ClientIP Operation Parameters{}.Name Parameters{}.Value

playbooks.name: Fraudulent wire already sent: recall and fund recovery
playbooks.summary: Use the moment finance realizes a wire went to a fraudulent account. The first hours decide whether funds can be frozen, so this playbook focuses on bank recall, law enforcement and evidence.

preparation: Keep the bank's 24-hour fraud desk number and relationship manager contact in the IR binder
Know how to file with the national cybercrime center and the financial fraud kill chain process
Notify the cyber insurer's claim line early, as policies often require it
identification: Record the wire reference, amount, value date, beneficiary bank, SWIFT or routing number and account
Collect the fraudulent instructions and full email headers that led to the wire
Identify who approved the wire and which verification steps were skipped
Check whether other payments went to the same beneficiary account
containment: Call the originating bank's fraud desk and request a recall and SWIFT gpi trace
File a complaint with the national cybercrime center the same day with the beneficiary details
Freeze further outbound wires from the affected account until approvals are reviewed
eradication: Find and fix the compromise that produced the fraudulent instructions
Remove the beneficiary from the treasury system's saved payee list
Preserve emails, call logs and approval records for law enforcement and the insurer
recovery: Track recall status with the bank daily and record every contact
Submit the insurance claim with the evidence package
Report the loss to auditors and the board as required
lessons: Record time from wire release to recall request
Identify the control that should have stopped the wire and make it mandatory
Run a tabletop on wire recall with treasury and the bank

splunk.title: Treasury wires to the beneficiary account
splunk.spl: index=treasury sourcetype=<treasury_audit> beneficiary_account=<ioc_account> earliest=-180d | table _time initiator approver amount currency beneficiary_name beneficiary_bank status

splunk.title: Mail mentioning the beneficiary details
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=ms:o365:reporting:messagetrace earliest=-30d Subject IN ("*wire*", "*payment*", "*bank details*") RecipientAddress IN (<finance_mailboxes>) | stats count by SenderAddress Subject FromIP

playbooks.name: Deepfake voice or video call from an executive requesting payment
playbooks.summary: Use when a staff member received a phone or video call where the voice or face of an executive appeared real but was likely synthetic, asking for a transfer or sensitive data.

preparation: Set a rule that no payment is approved on the strength of a call or video meeting alone
Agree on a shared code phrase or call-back process between executives and finance
Record which executives have large amounts of public audio or video online
identification: Record the call platform, caller ID or meeting link, time and duration
Ask the employee what was requested and what details the caller knew
Confirm with the real executive through a known number that they were not on the call
Collect any recording, meeting invite or chat transcript from the platform
Check for preceding emails or messages that set up the call
containment: Stop any payment or data transfer that came from the call
Block the meeting organizer account or phone number where possible
Alert finance and executive assistants that deepfake calls are active
eradication: Report the external meeting account to the meeting platform
Report the beneficiary account to the bank if payment details were given
Remove the meeting invite and follow-up messages from mailboxes
recovery: Give the employee clear support and confirm they will not be blamed
Brief all executives so they can warn their direct reports
Confirm with the bank that no transfer completed
lessons: Record whether the call-back rule existed and was used
Review the public audio and video of executives that could have been used for cloning
Add deepfake call scenarios to finance and assistant training

splunk.title: External meeting invites before the call
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=o365:management:activity Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation IN (MeetingParticipantDetail, MeetingDetail) earliest=-7d | search UserId=<suspect_user> OR Attendees{}.UPN=<suspect_user> | table _time UserId Operation Organizer.UPN JoinTime

splunk.title: Messages that set up the call
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.recipient="<suspect_user>" All_Email.subject IN ("*call*", "*meeting*", "*urgent*") NOT All_Email.src_user="*@<your_domain>" by All_Email.src_user All_Email.subject

playbooks.name: Unauthorized ACH payment initiated from the business banking portal
playbooks.summary: Use when an ACH batch or payment was created in online business banking without approval, usually by an attacker with a treasury user's stolen credentials.

preparation: Require dual control for creating and releasing ACH batches in the banking portal
Enable ACH positive pay or debit block with the bank
Use dedicated, hardened workstations for treasury banking sessions
identification: Pull the banking portal audit trail for the user who created and released the batch
Record each payee, amount, routing and account number in the unauthorized batch
Check the treasury user's workstation for remote access tools or banking malware
Compare portal login IPs with the company's egress IPs
containment: Call the bank to stop the batch or request reversal of entries not yet settled
Disable the treasury user's banking credentials and tokens
Isolate the treasury workstation in EDR
eradication: Reimage the treasury workstation and issue new banking tokens
Remove unknown payees or templates added to the banking portal
Reset the user's corporate and banking passwords from a clean device
recovery: Work with the bank on ACH return requests within the allowed window
Restore treasury access with dual control confirmed active
Reconcile all ACH activity for the past 30 days
lessons: Record whether dual control was enforced or bypassed
Add a detection for banking portal logins from IPs outside corporate egress
Review whether ACH limits per batch are set appropriately

splunk.title: Banking portal logins from non-corporate IPs
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*<bank_portal_domain>*" by Web.user Web.src Web.dest | search NOT Web.src IN (<corporate_egress_ips>)

splunk.title: Remote tools on the treasury workstation
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.dest=<host> Processes.process_name IN (anydesk.exe, teamviewer.exe, screenconnect*.exe, vncviewer.exe, rustdesk.exe) by Processes.user Processes.process_name

playbooks.name: Payment fraud demanding cryptocurrency transfer
playbooks.summary: Use when staff were pressured to pay an invoice, fine or vendor in cryptocurrency, or a treasury crypto wallet sent funds to an attacker address after a fraudulent request.

preparation: State in policy that the company does not pay vendors or fines in cryptocurrency unless treasury approves
Keep contacts for exchanges' compliance teams if the company holds crypto
Know which blockchain analytics service can trace transfers
identification: Record the wallet address, chain, amount, transaction hash and the request that led to it
Check whether the request came by email, chat or phone and from which identity
Trace the receiving address with a blockchain explorer to see if funds moved to an exchange
Find other staff who received the same payment demand
containment: Contact the receiving exchange's compliance team with the transaction hash to request a freeze
Block further transfers from the corporate wallet until approvals are reviewed
Block the sender identity used for the request
eradication: Rotate keys or API credentials for any corporate exchange account used
Remove the attacker wallet from any saved address book
Report the theft to law enforcement with the transaction details
recovery: Track freeze and recovery requests with the exchange
Restore wallet operations with dual signing or multi-sig in place
Tell affected staff the outcome and next steps
lessons: Record why a crypto payment was possible without treasury sign-off
Add a watch for crypto wallet addresses appearing in inbound mail to finance
Decide whether corporate wallets need multi-signature for all outbound transfers

splunk.title: Inbound mail mentioning crypto payment
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.subject IN ("*bitcoin*", "*BTC*", "*USDT*", "*crypto*", "*wallet*") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject

splunk.title: Exchange API activity from corporate accounts
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=<exchange_audit> action IN (withdrawal, address_add, api_key_create) earliest=-14d | table _time user action asset amount destination_address src_ip

playbooks.name: Fake executive request for employee W-2 or tax records
playbooks.summary: Use when HR or payroll received a request, often from someone posing as the CEO or CFO, for all employees' W-2 forms or tax data, and you must know if PII was sent.

preparation: Require that bulk employee tax data only goes out through approved, encrypted systems
Set a DLP rule for outbound mail containing many SSNs or W-2 attachments
Tell HR and payroll that executives will never ask for W-2 bundles by email
identification: Confirm with the named executive by phone that they did not make the request
Find out if anyone replied with W-2 PDFs, spreadsheets or a payroll export
Check sent items and DLP logs for outbound mail with SSNs to the attacker address
Count the employees whose data was in any file sent
containment: Block the reply-to address and the sending domain
Ask the receiving provider to suspend the attacker mailbox and preserve data
Recall the message if it went to an internal or same-tenant address
eradication: Notify the tax authority's phishing reporting address about the data theft
Prepare employee breach notifications and identity protection with legal
Remove the lure and replies from HR mailboxes
recovery: Offer credit monitoring and identity protection PINs to affected employees
Watch for fraudulent tax filings reported by employees and track them
Brief HR and payroll on the attempt and the new rule
lessons: Record whether DLP fired on the outbound file and why it did not block
Add a detection for external replies from HR containing spreadsheets or PDFs with SSN patterns
Review state breach notification deadlines and whether they were met

splunk.title: Outbound mail from HR with attachments
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src_user IN (<hr_mailboxes>) NOT All_Email.recipient="*@<your_domain>" All_Email.file_name IN ("*.pdf", "*.xlsx", "*.csv", "*.zip") by All_Email.recipient All_Email.file_name All_Email.subject

splunk.title: DLP matches for SSN patterns
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=o365:management:activity Operation=DlpRuleMatch earliest=-7d | search PolicyDetails{}.Rules{}.ConditionsMatched.SensitiveInformation{}.SensitiveInformationTypeName="*Social Security*" | table _time UserId ExceptionInfo.Reason PolicyDetails{}.PolicyName

playbooks.name: Accounts payable mailbox compromised and used to redirect payments
playbooks.summary: Use when an attacker controls your own AP or finance clerk mailbox and is replying to vendors, editing invoices or approving bank changes from inside the company.

preparation: Require phishing-resistant MFA for all finance staff
Alert on inbox rules in finance mailboxes that match vendor names or payment keywords
Keep a list of finance mailboxes and shared mailboxes for scoped searches
identification: Review sign-ins to the AP mailbox for new IPs and session reuse
Read sent items for messages to vendors that change bank details or payment dates
Check MailItemsAccessed for the volume of finance mail read by the attacker
List invoices or payment approvals actioned by the account since compromise
Check shared AP mailboxes the user can access for the same activity
containment: Revoke sessions, reset the password and block sign-in for the AP user
Freeze the next payment run until each change made by the account is checked
Remove the attacker's inbox rules on the mailbox and any shared mailboxes
eradication: Contact every vendor the attacker emailed and tell them which messages were fraudulent
Revert vendor master changes approved by the account
Remove attacker MFA methods and devices
recovery: Release the payment run after finance validates each payee
Re-enable the AP user with phishing-resistant MFA
Recall any payments that went to changed accounts
lessons: Record how the AP account was first compromised and link to the phishing case
Add a detection for finance accounts sending mail to vendors from new IPs
Require a second approver for any vendor master change made by AP staff

splunk.title: Mail sent by the AP account to vendors
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src_user="<suspect_user>" NOT All_Email.recipient="*@<your_domain>" by All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject _time span=1h

splunk.title: Mailbox items accessed by attacker session
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=o365:management:activity Operation=MailItemsAccessed MailboxOwnerUPN=<suspect_user> ClientIPAddress=<ioc_ip> | stats sum(OperationCount) as items count by ClientIPAddress ClientInfoString

splunk.title: Vendor master changes approved by the account
splunk.spl: index=erp sourcetype=<erp_audit> user=<suspect_user> object=vendor_master earliest=-30d | table _time vendor_id field old_value new_value

playbooks.name: Customers paid fake invoices sent in the company's name
playbooks.summary: Use when customers report paying invoices that looked like yours but carried a different bank account, sent from a lookalike domain or a compromised billing mailbox.

preparation: Print the company's verified bank details and a call-to-verify notice on every invoice
Keep DMARC at reject for billing domains
Give the customer support team a script for customers reporting suspicious invoices
identification: Collect the fake invoices, headers and bank details from each reporting customer
Determine whether they came from a lookalike domain or your real billing mailbox
Check the billing mailbox and invoicing platform for compromise if the domain was real
Find out how the attacker knew which customers had open invoices
containment: Contact the receiving bank with the fraudulent account details for each customer report
Block the lookalike domain and request registrar suspension
Notify customers with open invoices that bank details have not changed
eradication: Secure the billing mailbox or invoicing platform if it was the source
Report the fraud to law enforcement with all customer reports
Remove any data exports or API keys the attacker created in the invoicing platform
recovery: Agree with finance and legal how to handle outstanding balances for defrauded customers
Confirm DMARC and billing domain protections are in place
Follow up with each affected customer on recall status
lessons: Record how customers spotted the fraud and how many paid before noticing
Add a detection for lookalikes of billing domains in domain monitoring
Consider moving customers to a payment portal so invoices do not carry bank details

splunk.title: Invoicing platform exports and API key changes
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=<billing_platform_audit> action IN (export_customers, export_invoices, api_key_created, user_login) earliest=-30d | stats count values(action) as actions by user src_ip

splunk.title: Outbound billing mail volume by recipient domain
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.src_user="<billing_mailbox>" by All_Email.recipient All_Email.src_ip _time span=1d

playbooks.name: Purchase order fraud: suppliers shipping goods to impersonators
playbooks.summary: Use when suppliers report receiving purchase orders in your company's name, from lookalike domains, for goods on credit terms shipped to addresses you do not control.

preparation: Publish the official procurement email domain and PO format on the supplier portal
Give suppliers a phone number to confirm unexpected large orders
Monitor for lookalike domains of procurement domains
identification: Collect the fake POs, sender addresses, shipping addresses and named buyers from suppliers
Check the ERP to confirm no matching PO numbers exist
Identify whether real employee names were used as the buyer
Search for credit applications filed with suppliers in your company's name
containment: Tell the affected suppliers to halt shipments and cancel the orders
Block the lookalike domains at the gateway and request suspension
Notify carriers or freight forwarders of the delivery addresses if shipments are in transit
eradication: Report the delivery addresses to law enforcement
Ask suppliers to revoke credit accounts opened in your name
Warn named employees that their names are being used
recovery: Send a supplier advisory describing how to verify genuine orders
Confirm with legal that the company is not liable for the fraudulent orders
Track supplier reports for further attempts over 60 days
lessons: Record how many suppliers were contacted before the first report
Add the lookalike patterns to domain monitoring
Review public pages that list procurement staff and their emails

splunk.title: Supplier replies to lookalike addresses
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.recipient="*@<lookalike_domain>" OR All_Email.src_user="*@<lookalike_domain>" by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject

splunk.title: Inbound supplier mail referencing PO numbers
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.recipient IN (<procurement_mailboxes>) All_Email.subject IN ("*PO*", "*purchase order*", "*credit application*") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.subject

playbooks.name: Mailed vendor check stolen, altered or counterfeited
playbooks.summary: Use when a check the company mailed was intercepted and washed, re-payee'd or copied, and the bank shows cleared items that do not match the check register.

preparation: Enroll disbursement accounts in check positive pay with payee name matching
Reconcile the check register against bank-cleared items daily
Use security paper and tamper-evident envelopes for mailed checks
identification: Compare cleared check images from the bank with the issue file for payee, amount and date
Record the check numbers, depositing bank and endorsement on each fraudulent item
Confirm with the intended vendor that they never received the check
Look for patterns, such as checks mailed from the same postal facility or route
containment: Ask the bank to return the fraudulent items under the positive pay or UCC timeline
Place stop payments on other outstanding checks mailed in the same batch
Pause mailed checks from the affected account
eradication: Report the theft to the postal inspection service
Close the compromised account and open a new one if counterfeits used its numbers
File a police report for the insurer and the bank
recovery: Reissue payment to the vendor by ACH after verifying their bank details by phone
Update the vendor master to prefer electronic payment
Track bank reimbursement of the fraudulent items
lessons: Record whether positive pay flagged the items and whether payee matching was enabled
Measure how many vendors are still paid by mailed check
Set a target date to move most vendors to electronic payment

splunk.title: Cleared items not matching the issue file
splunk.spl: index=treasury sourcetype=<bank_cleared_items> earliest=-30d | join type=left check_number [search index=treasury sourcetype=<check_issue_file> earliest=-90d | rename amount as issued_amount payee as issued_payee] | where amount!=issued_amount OR payee!=issued_payee OR isnull(issued_amount) | table check_number issued_payee payee issued_amount amount deposit_bank

splunk.title: Positive pay exceptions
splunk.spl: index=treasury sourcetype=<positive_pay_exceptions> earliest=-14d | stats count values(reason) as reasons by account check_number decision

playbooks.name: Fake vendor added to the ERP and paid for invoices
playbooks.summary: Use when a vendor record was created for a company that does not exist or is controlled by a fraudster, and invoices from it were approved and paid.

preparation: Require tax ID, bank letter and business registry checks before vendor activation
Separate the roles that create vendors and approve their invoices
Log vendor creation and first payment events in the ERP audit trail
identification: Pull the vendor creation record and note who created and approved it
Check the vendor's tax ID, address and phone against public business registries
List all invoices and payments made to the vendor and who approved each
Check whether the vendor's bank account matches an employee's direct deposit account
Find out whether the request came by email from outside or from an internal user
containment: Block the vendor record in the ERP so no further payments can run
Hold any open invoices from the vendor
Preserve ERP logs and approval emails for the investigation
eradication: Ask the bank to recall recent payments to the vendor's account
Escalate to HR and legal if an employee was involved in the setup
Remove the requester's vendor creation rights if they abused them
recovery: Re-verify all vendors created in the last 90 days against the onboarding checklist
Report the fraud to auditors
Restore normal vendor creation with the new checks enforced
lessons: Record which onboarding check was skipped
Add an ERP report matching vendor bank accounts against payroll accounts
Track the time between vendor creation and first payment for anomalies

splunk.title: Vendor creation and first payments
splunk.spl: index=erp sourcetype=<erp_audit> (action=vendor_create OR action=payment_released) vendor_id=<vendor_id> | table _time action user approver amount bank_account

splunk.title: Recently created vendors with quick payments
splunk.spl: index=erp sourcetype=<erp_audit> action=vendor_create earliest=-90d | stats min(_time) as created by vendor_id user | join vendor_id [search index=erp sourcetype=<erp_audit> action=payment_released earliest=-90d | stats min(_time) as first_paid sum(amount) as total by vendor_id] | eval days=round((first_paid-created)/86400,1) | where days<14

playbooks.name: Corporate purchasing card details phished and misused
playbooks.summary: Use when an employee entered a corporate card number on a fake site or invoice page and unauthorized charges are appearing on the card program.

preparation: Set merchant category and per-transaction limits on corporate cards
Enable real-time transaction alerts to cardholders
Keep the card issuer's fraud line in the finance contact list
identification: Get the list of unauthorized transactions from the card program portal
Ask the cardholder where they last entered the card number and when
Check proxy logs for the cardholder visiting the phishing page
Find other cardholders who visited the same page
containment: Cancel the card with the issuer and request a replacement
Block the phishing domain at the proxy
Lower limits temporarily on cards for staff who received the same lure
eradication: File disputes for each unauthorized transaction
Check whether the cardholder also entered their corporate password on the page
Report the phishing site to its host
recovery: Issue the replacement card and update recurring vendor charges
Confirm disputes are credited in the next statement
Remind cardholders how real vendors request card payment
lessons: Record whether transaction alerts reached the cardholder in time
Add a detection for proxy visits to payment pages on newly registered domains
Review whether virtual single-use cards should replace physical cards for online purchases

splunk.title: Cardholders who reached the phishing payment page
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count values(Web.http_method) as methods from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*<ioc_domain>*" by Web.user Web.src

splunk.title: Card program alerts for affected cards
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=<card_program_audit> card_last4=<card_last4> earliest=-30d | table _time merchant mcc amount currency status

playbooks.name: Fraudster posing as a customer requests a refund to a new account
playbooks.summary: Use when someone impersonating a customer asks for a refund, credit balance or overpayment to be sent to a different bank account than the original payment came from.

preparation: Require refunds to go back to the original payment method unless the customer verifies by phone
Train accounts receivable to spot changed contact details on refund requests
Log refund approvals in the billing system
identification: Compare the requester's address and phone with the customer record
Contact the customer on the number on file to confirm the request
Check whether the customer's real mailbox may be compromised by reviewing headers
Search for other refund requests with the same bank account or sender domain
containment: Cancel the pending refund
Flag the customer account for manual review of any changes
Block the requester's domain if it is a lookalike
eradication: Tell the customer if their mailbox appears compromised
Report the bank account to your bank's fraud desk
Remove any updated contact details the fraudster added to the customer record
recovery: Issue the genuine refund to the original payment method if one was due
Confirm the customer record matches verified details
Record the attempt in the fraud register
lessons: Record whether the original-method rule was in place and followed
Add a report for refunds sent to accounts that never paid the company
Share the pattern with the customer support team

splunk.title: Refund requests to accounts receivable
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.recipient IN (<ar_mailboxes>) All_Email.subject IN ("*refund*", "*overpayment*", "*credit balance*") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.subject

splunk.title: Refunds to new bank accounts
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=<billing_audit> action=refund_issued earliest=-90d | stats count sum(amount) as total by customer_id refund_account original_payment_account | where refund_account!=original_payment_account

playbooks.name: Lookalike domain inserted into an ongoing payment email thread
playbooks.summary: Use when someone swapped a participant's address for a lookalike in a live finance thread, so replies about payment now go to the attacker while the conversation history looks intact.

preparation: Configure the gateway to flag first-time senders with domains one edit away from known contacts
Teach finance staff to check the full address, not just the display name, on payment threads
Monitor domain registrations similar to top suppliers and partners
identification: Identify the exact message where the address changed to the lookalike
Determine which side leaked the thread by checking whether attacker-quoted text came from your mailbox or the partner's
List every message sent to the lookalike and whether it contained payment or banking details
Check your participants' mailboxes for compromise if the thread was stolen from your side
containment: Stop any payment based on details given in the hijacked thread
Block the lookalike domain and purge its messages
Start a new thread with the real partner by phone to confirm the true state of the deal
eradication: Reset the compromised mailbox on whichever side leaked the thread
Request suspension of the lookalike domain at the registrar
Notify the partner's security team of the lookalike
recovery: Re-confirm all bank details in the deal by phone before payment
Add the partner's real addresses to a verified contact list for finance
Recall any payment already sent
lessons: Record how many replies went to the lookalike before discovery
Add a detection for replies in an existing thread to a domain first seen that day
Decide whether external senders with lookalike domains should be blocked outright

splunk.title: Messages to the lookalike in the thread
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=ms:o365:reporting:messagetrace (RecipientAddress="*@<lookalike_domain>" OR SenderAddress="*@<lookalike_domain>") | table _time SenderAddress RecipientAddress Subject Status

splunk.title: First-seen sender domains replying to finance
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as first count from datamodel=Email where All_Email.recipient IN (<finance_mailboxes>) All_Email.subject="RE:*" by All_Email.src_user | where first>relative_time(now(), "-1d") | convert ctime(first)
